note.note:
Action Plan:
1. Emergency response activated: ambulance called to attend ongoing central chest discomfort with concerning cardiac features.  
2. Patient instructed to wait near open front door for rapid paramedic access.  
3. Clinician remained on video line to monitor patient until paramedics arrive and will hand-over history, risk factors, and aspirin allergy.  
4. Paramedics to obtain on-scene 12-lead ECG and transport to hospital for definitive evaluation and management of suspected acute coronary syndrome.  
5. Patient advised to inform all treating staff of his mild aspirin allergy; potential need for aspirin despite allergy discussed.  
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• 60-year-old male (DOB 08 Aug 1958) presents with first episode of central chest pressure that began ~2 h ago while gardening (light activity) and is still present.  
  – Character: “someone sitting on my chest,” diffuse, mid-chest.  
  – Radiation: left arm and shoulder.  
  – Associated symptoms: shortness of breath, nausea (no vomiting), diaphoresis, sense of rapid heartbeat (likely anxiety-related).  
• No previous similar episodes.  
• Past Medical History: Hypertension. No diabetes; cholesterol never checked.  
• Medications: Not documented.  
• Allergies: Aspirin – causes mild swelling (non-life-threatening).  
• Social History:  
  – Smokes ~10 cigarettes/day for 15 years.  
  – Alcohol: ~7–8 pints beer/week.  
  – Low physical activity; overweight (self-reported).  
  – Lives alone; restaurant owner (sushi shop).  
• Family History: Father died of myocardial infarction around age 60; mother with unspecified heart disease.  

Objective:
• No formal vitals recorded during telehealth session.  
• General appearance on video: sweaty, visibly short of breath, speaking in full sentences.  
• No physical examination possible via telehealth.  
• Investigations: None yet; paramedics to perform ECG on arrival.

Assessment & Plan:
1. Acute chest pain with cardiovascular risk factors  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction vs. unstable angina) – DDx item “Acute coronary syndrome,” likelihood High.  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Aortic dissection – DDx likelihood Medium (less typical “tearing” pain, no back radiation).  
     • Pulmonary embolism – DDx likelihood Low–Medium (SOB, tachycardia sensation but pain non-pleuritic, no DVT risk).  
     • Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease / oesophageal spasm – DDx likelihood Low (lacks typical GI triggers, has diaphoresis & arm radiation).  
     • Panic/anxiety attack – DDx likelihood Low (age, risk factors, typical anginal features).  
   - Investigations planned: Pre-hospital 12-lead ECG; hospital evaluation with serial cardiac enzymes, CXR, basic labs as per ACS protocol (to be arranged by receiving hospital).  
   - Treatment planned: Immediate EMS transport; oxygen, nitrates, analgesia, dual antiplatelet therapy to be considered by ED/cardiology team with caution re aspirin allergy; full ACS protocol on arrival.  
   - Relevant referrals: Emergency Department / cardiology team on arrival; possible cath lab activation depending on ECG/biomarkers.

2. Chronic cardiovascular risk factor management (smoking, hypertension, overweight) – deferred  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Established cardiovascular risk factors contributing to suspected ACS.  
   - Plan: Address smoking cessation, hypertension optimisation, weight management, lipid profile once acute event stabilised (not actioned in this emergent call).

Quality checks:
• Missing but expected: full medication list, current antihypertensives, baseline vitals, previous ECGs, cholesterol level.  
• Internal conflict: Doctor initially mis-estimated patient’s age as “about fifty” while patient is 60 – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio; minimal background noise; no inaudible sections.
